title: The Afternoon Brief: College Eligibility Bans Now Collide With Court Orders
dek: The Big Ten and SEC moved to bar athletes with professional experience from college competition, setting conference rules directly against a Louisiana court order that has already sent players back to campuses, while the Astros' front office and a series of injury reports rounded out the day.
author: GoCheckMySports
key_fact: The Big Ten and SEC eligibility bans now sit in direct conflict with a Louisiana court order allowing NFL-affiliated players back into college sports, with an August 31 hearing set to test which authority holds.
bottom_line: The day's defining story is the widening collision between the Big Ten and SEC's new eligibility bans on players with professional experience and a Louisiana court order that has already sent players like Dae'Quan Wright back to college competition. That fight will be tested at an August 31 injunction hearing, which lands the same day as the NFL's roster cutdown deadline, a date reporting suggests could generate more eligibility litigation. Elsewhere, the Astros confirmed general manager Dana Brown's departure with owner Jim Crane taking interim control, a BMJ study documented CTE in 215 of 235 deceased NFL players studied, and injury reports touched the Bengals, Giants, Ravens, and Trail Blazers. The honest read is that today's reporting establishes the legal and organizational facts clearly but leaves outcomes, medical severity, and further litigation genuinely open.
body: The day's central thread is a legal collision building around college eligibility. The Big Ten voted unanimously Tuesday to prohibit football players who signed professional contracts, appeared on a professional roster, or declared for the NFL Draft as underclassmen without withdrawing from competing at member schools. The SEC followed the same night with an identical football rule, extended to basketball players with NBA or WNBA experience. Both conferences are acting directly against a Louisiana state court's temporary restraining order that already allowed a group of players, including Cleveland Browns tight end Dae'Quan Wright, to return to college after NFL preseason participation, provided they terminated their contracts and returned any money earned. Wright has since signed with LSU. The court's order runs until a hearing on August 31, which will test whether conference rules can hold against a judicial order that points the other way. The ACC and Big 12 are reportedly in similar conversations, and The American is considering a conference-wide ban, while sports attorney Darren Heitner reported inquiries from at least a dozen players or representatives about filing further lawsuits.

Outside that story, the day's other news moved in smaller, separate lanes. The Houston Astros parted ways with general manager Dana Brown on August 24, with owner Jim Crane assuming interim control of baseball operations and dividing Brown's duties among assistant GMs Charles Cook, Gavin Dickey, and Connor Huff, plus senior advisor Jeff Bagwell. It is the second GM turnover under Crane's ownership in four years; he performed a similar interim role after firing James Click days after the 2022 World Series. An MLB.com report of the same separation could not be independently verified beyond the attribution itself, but the broader facts of the departure and Crane's assumption of interim duties are established by Front Office Sports reporting.

Injuries touched several sports. Bengals receiver Ja'Marr Chase walked off practice on his own power after what he described as a minor knee hyperextension, saying he could have kept practicing had the team allowed it. Giants slot receiver Calvin Austin suffered an apparent serious knee injury without contact during a 1-on-1 drill, though no official diagnosis or medical timeline has been provided. Ravens center Danny Pinter tore his patellar tendon in a joint practice with the Vikings and was placed on injured reserve, ending his season and pushing Baltimore toward Jovaughn Gwyn and Ethan Pocic at center. Trail Blazers guard Shaedon Sharpe tore his meniscus in an offseason workout and faces a roughly six-month recovery, likely returning in late February or early March. Separately, a British Medical Journal study found chronic traumatic encephalopathy in 215 of 235 deceased NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021 and donated their brains to research, establishing a conservative minimum prevalence of 24.5% among that group, with researchers pointing to cumulative head impacts across youth, high school, and college levels as a driver.

On the business side, prediction-market platform Kalshi signed brand partnerships with the Braves, Red Sox, Dodgers, Padres, and Giants, bringing the total number of MLB clubs with prediction-market deals to seven, just months after Polymarket became MLB's exclusive league-level partner. The 3-on-3 league Unrivaled announced a Series C valuing the company at $650 million, up from $340 million in September, with players holding roughly 30% ownership. The NWSL signed Roku to stream its Sunday night package starting August 30, replacing the collapsed Victory+ arrangement. The PGA Tour announced it will replace the Tour Championship's 22-year run at East Lake with a two-week match play format beginning in 2028. In Chicago, Sky owner Michael Alter banned Enes Kanter Freedom indefinitely from Wintrust Arena after his ejection during Sunday's game against the Fever following an exchange with guard Natasha Cloud; league sources separately told Front Office Sports that Kanter Freedom and Royce White are not eligible to play in the WNBA. Rugby league great Sir Billy Boston, the first player knighted in the sport's history, died at 92.

Why these things are happening varies by story. The eligibility fight is driven by conferences trying to close a legal opening before it widens, with the NFL's August 31 roster cutdown, when teams trim from 90 to 53 players, expected to generate more eligibility claimants. The Astros' shakeup follows a pattern Crane has used before. The injury cluster across the NFL and NBA has no stated common cause beyond the ordinary attrition of camp and offseason training; the reporting does not connect them.

What to watch in the coming days centers on the August 31 Louisiana injunction hearing, which will determine whether the court order survives against the new conference bans, and the same date's NFL roster cutdown, which could produce more players seeking similar relief. Also worth tracking: whether the ACC, Big 12, or The American formally adopt bans matching the Big Ten and SEC, any Bengals or Giants medical updates on Chase and Austin, Sharpe's recovery timeline in Portland, and whether Houston moves toward a permanent general manager or further consolidates authority under Crane.
